screens.title: Minimum Cluster Size and Topology
screens.narratorSegment: A core principle of Redis Cluster is quorum-based failover. In plain terms, the cluster needs at least three masters so that a majority can be reached during failover decisions. If you run fewer than three masters, the cluster cannot reliably elect a new master when one fails. For high availability in production, each master should have at least one replica. That means a minimal robust deployment is three masters plus three replicas. The replicas follow different masters so the loss of one physical host does not remove both a master and its only replica. A common test topology uses six instances on one machine with ports 7000–7005: masters on 7000–7002 and replicas on 7003–7005. This configuration lets you observe replica promotion and slot redistribution without needing multiple hosts. A common misconception is that replicas alone provide quorum — they do not. Only masters participate in voting for failover. Key takeaway: plan for at least three masters and pair replicas across different hosts when possible. How would your promotion strategy change if two masters failed at once? Minimum Cluster Size and Topology means at least three masters are needed so a majority can be reached for failover decisions; replicas supply availability but do not form quorum.. In practical terms, why three masters and replicas matter for failover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Minimum Cluster Size
Core Concept

Three masters, paired replicas

Redis Cluster requires a minimum of three master nodes for quorum. Each master should have at least one replica for high availability. This pairing preserves failover capability and allows promotion when a master fails.

Concrete example

Test on one host using ports 7000–7005. Assign masters to 7000, 7001, 7002 and replicas to 7003, 7004, 7005.

Common misconception

Replicas do not participate in quorum voting. They hold copies but cannot elect a master unless promoted as a master during maintenance.

Key Takeaway

Design clusters with at least three masters and place replicas on separate hosts for true resilience.

Topology Preview
7000
Master A
7001
Master B
7002
Master C
7003
Replica of 7000
7004
Replica of 7001
7005
Replica of 7002
Why separate hosts?

Placing a master and its replica on different hosts ensures a single host failure doesn't remove both copies. This reduces correlated failures and keeps the cluster operational.

screens.title: Configure instances for cluster mode
screens.narratorSegment: Before you create a cluster, every Redis instance must be configured for cluster mode. The three mandatory settings you will use are cluster-enabled yes, cluster-config-file with a node-unique filename, and cluster-node-timeout set to a reasonable value. The cluster-config-file is where each node stores its local view of peers and slot assignments; Redis manages it automatically, so do not edit it while the node runs. For a test topology on one machine, create six redis. conf files that differ by port, pidfile, logfile, dbfilename, dir, and cluster-config-file. A concrete example is a redis-7000. conf that contains port 7000, daemonize yes, dir./cluster-data/7000, cluster-enabled yes, and cluster-config-file nodes-7000. conf. After you start the instances, they will write their nodes files and begin gossip. A common mistake is forgetting cluster-enabled yes or pointing multiple instances to the same cluster-config-file. Both lead to confused node identities. Key takeaway: unique node files and enabled cluster mode are required before you run redis-cli --cluster create. Configure instances for cluster mode means set cluster-enabled yes and give each instance its distinct cluster-config-file so nodes keep separate identities.. In practical terms, essential redis.conf settings for cluster participation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Configure Cluster Mode
Process

Essential redis.conf settings

Each instance must have cluster-enabled yes, a unique cluster-config-file, and a cluster-node-timeout. These settings let the node join the cluster and persist its local topology.

Example configuration fragment
port 7000
daemonize yes
pidfile /var/run/redis-7000.pid
logfile "/var/log/redis-7000.log"
dir ./cluster-data/7000
cluster-enabled yes
cluster-config-file nodes-7000.conf
cluster-node-timeout 5000
appendonly yes
Concrete tip

Give each instance a different cluster-config-file, e.g., nodes-7000.conf. Do not reuse the same filename across processes.

Key Takeaway

Unique node identities and cluster-enabled yes are required before creating a cluster.

Checklist
  • Create separate directory per node: cluster-data/7000 ... 7005
  • Set port and pidfile per instance
  • Use cluster-enabled yes in each redis.conf
  • Provide cluster-config-file nodes-<port>.conf for each
  • Choose cluster-node-timeout like 5000 ms for tests
Common mistake

Pointing multiple instances to the same cluster-config-file will break node identity and prevent the cluster from forming correctly.

screens.title: Start instances and create the cluster
screens.narratorSegment: Once your redis. conf files are ready, start each Redis instance with redis-server pointing to its configuration. After six instances are up for a 3-master, 3-replica test, use redis-cli --cluster create with the addresses of all nodes and the --cluster-replicas flag. For example, run redis-cli --cluster create 127.0.0.1:7000 127.0.0.1:7001 127.0.0.1:7002 127.0.0.1:7003 127.0.0.1:7004 127.0.0.1:7005 --cluster-replicas 1 and then type yes when prompted. The tool proposes a mapping of slots to masters and assigns replicas to masters automatically. The redis-cli cluster helper handles slot assignment so you do not manually choose slot ranges during a simple create. A useful hands-on check is to connect with redis-cli -p 7000 and run CLUSTER NODES to see roles and assigned slots. A common misconception is that --cluster create only needs master addresses; in practice give all nodes you want in the cluster and set --cluster-replicas to control replica counts. After creation, watch nodes write their nodes-. conf files and begin exchanging gossip messages. Start instances and create the cluster means redis-cli --cluster create assigns hash slots and pairs replicas when you provide node addresses and --cluster-replicas.. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Create Cluster
Code Walkthrough

Start instances and run create

Start each server with its redis.conf and run the cluster create command with all node addresses and --cluster-replicas to assign replicas automatically.

# start each instance
redis-server redis-7000.conf
redis-server redis-7001.conf
...

# create the cluster
redis-cli --cluster create 127.0.0.1:7000 127.0.0.1:7001 127.0.0.1:7002 \
  127.0.0.1:7003 127.0.0.1:7004 127.0.0.1:7005 --cluster-replicas 1
# type yes when prompted
Verification
redis-cli -p 7000
> CLUSTER NODES
redis-cli --cluster check 127.0.0.1:7000
Key Takeaway

Provide all instance addresses to the create command and use --cluster-replicas to control replica assignment.

Practical notes
  • Include both master and replica addresses during create for a smooth layout.
  • Type yes to accept slot and replica assignments proposed by the helper.
  • After create, nodes will exchange gossip and persist nodes-PORT.conf files.
Misconception

Do not assume redis-cli --cluster create performs live data movement beyond initial slot assignment — it sets the initial distribution so your cluster starts with each master owning a set of slots.

screens.title: Masters vs Replicas
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between master and replica is fundamental. A master owns a subset of hash slots and accepts writes for keys mapped to those slots; replicas hold copies of a master's data and remain read-capable depending on your client setup. Masters participate in quorum voting used for failover decisions; replicas do not vote. In practice, replicas are promoted to masters when their master fails and the cluster elects a replica that can take over. An important operational contrast is that only masters have assigned hash slots — when you add a new master it initially has no slots until you reshard. A common operational error is trying to remove a master without migrating its slots first; the del-node operation will fail if the master still holds slots. Concrete example: if master on port 7001 fails, its replica on 7004 can be promoted; you should verify promotion by checking CLUSTER NODES and that the new master now lists the slot ranges. Key takeaway: know which nodes hold slots and which can be promoted. Masters vs Replicas means masters hold slots and vote for failover; replicas store copies and can be promoted but do not form quorum themselves.. In practical terms, roles, responsibilities, and what each participates in. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Masters vs Replicas
Master

Owns hash slots

Masters accept writes for keys mapped to their assigned slots. They participate in quorum and can be the target of replica promotion or failover voting.

Assigned slots: yes
Votes for failover: yes
Replica promotion target: yes
Replica

Holds a copy

Replicas store copies of a master's data and can serve reads. They do not vote in quorum but can be promoted to master if needed.

Assigned slots: no
Votes for failover: no
Promotion to master: possible
Operational example

If master 7001 fails, its replica (for example 7004) is eligible for promotion. Verify with CLUSTER NODES to see the new role and slot ownership after election.

screens.title: Adding nodes to a running cluster
screens.narratorSegment: Adding a node to an existing cluster is a two-step idea: join and then assign responsibilities. Use redis-cli --cluster add-node new_ip:new_port existing_ip:existing_port to make the new process join the cluster. If you are adding a replica, append --cluster-slave and provide --cluster-master-id to indicate which master it should follow. After joining, a newly added master will have no hash slots, so you must reshard some slots from existing masters to the newcomer to give it data and load. A concrete example: to add a new master at 10.0.0.10:7006, run redis-cli --cluster add-node 10.0.0.10:7006 127.0.0.1:7000. To add a replica of master 7001 you would run the add-node command with --cluster-slave and the master node id obtained from CLUSTER NODES. A common oversight is failing to reshard after adding a master, leaving it idle. Key takeaway: join first, then rebalance slots to utilize added capacity. Adding nodes to a running cluster means add-node integrates a new process; resharding moves slots so the added master holds data and contributes to load distribution.. In practical terms, how to add masters and replicas using redis-cli --cluster add-node. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Add Nodes
Architecture

Add master or replica to cluster

Use add-node to join, then reshard slots to give the new master data. For replicas include --cluster-slave and the master's node id.

# add a new master
redis-cli --cluster add-node 10.0.0.10:7006 127.0.0.1:7000

# add a replica for a specific master (escape angle brackets)
redis-cli --cluster add-node 10.0.0.11:7007 127.0.0.1:7000 --cluster-slave --cluster-master-id <master_node_id>
Practical note

Obtain the master node id via CLUSTER NODES before adding a replica so you can point the replica to the right master.

Example scenario

You want to expand capacity. Add a new master process, then reshard roughly equal slot ranges from current masters to the new master to spread load.

Checkpoints
  • Run add-node and confirm CLUSTER NODES shows joined node.
  • Run redis-cli --cluster reshard to move slots to the new master.
  • Use redis-cli --cluster check to confirm balanced slots.

screens.title: Resharding hash slots
screens.narratorSegment: Resharding is the process of moving hash slots between masters to rebalance data or to populate a newly added master. Use redis-cli --cluster reshard target_node to begin an interactive flow. The tool asks how many slots to move, which source nodes to take them from, and confirms the target. Redis migrates data slot by slot, ensuring keys in those slots are copied and ownership changes atomically for each slot. In practice, pick a conservative number of slots to move in one operation to avoid large resource spikes. A concrete example is adding a new master and moving roughly one third of slots from existing masters to the newcomer. Misconceptions include thinking reshard moves data instantly; it proceeds slot-by-slot and can be resource-intensive. Always perform resharding during low traffic, monitor replication lag, and use redis-cli --cluster check after resharding to confirm slots are distributed as expected. Key takeaway: reshard deliberately, validate after, and plan for resource usage during migration. Resharding hash slots means resharding moves slots incrementally. plan operations to limit impact and verify with cluster checks after migration.. In practical terms, move slots safely using redis-cli --cluster reshard. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Resharding
Process

Reshard using redis-cli --cluster reshard

Start an interactive reshard operation. Specify the number of slots to move and choose the source masters. The helper migrates slots one at a time to preserve consistency.

# start resharding (interactive)
redis-cli --cluster reshard 127.0.0.1:7000

# follow prompts: how many slots, source node ids, target node id
Operational caution

Resharding can be resource-intensive. Perform during off-peak hours and monitor replication lag and CPU to avoid unexpected impact.

Reshard checklist
  1. Decide how many slots to move
  2. Identify source and target master node ids via CLUSTER NODES
  3. Run redis-cli --cluster reshard and confirm prompts
  4. Monitor replication lag and run redis-cli --cluster check when finished
Misconception

Resharding is not instantaneous and can take time proportional to moved keys. Treat it like a maintenance window when possible.

screens.title: Removing nodes safely
screens.narratorSegment: Removing a node requires care because masters may hold slots that must be redistributed first. The redis-cli --cluster del-node command removes a node from the cluster, but it will reject removal if the node still owns slots. Therefore the safe procedure is: reshard all slots away from the master you plan to remove, verify it has zero assigned slots via CLUSTER NODES, and then run del-node with the target node id. If you mistakenly try to remove a master with slots, the tool will fail and abort. For replicas the removal is simpler: a replica without slots can be removed and replaced more easily, but it is still good practice to ensure the cluster remains balanced. A concrete example is to reshard slots from master with id abc123..., confirm CLUSTER NODES shows no slots, then run redis-cli --cluster del-node 127.0.0.1:7001 abc123... Always perform such maintenance during low traffic and ensure you have backups or snapshots if data loss would be critical. Key takeaway: migrate slots before removing a master. Removing nodes safely means del-node only succeeds if a master has no assigned slots. reshard first to move all slots away.. In practical terms, del-node and the requirement to migrate slots first. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Remove Nodes
Process

Reshard away slots, then del-node

Do not attempt to delete a master before migrating its slots. The del-node operation will fail if slots remain.

# reshard all slots away from master <master_id>
redis-cli --cluster reshard 127.0.0.1:7000
# follow prompts to move all slots to other masters

# once the master has zero slots
redis-cli --cluster del-node 127.0.0.1:7000 <master_id>
Operational tip

Confirm slot-less state with CLUSTER NODES before del-node to avoid failed removal attempts.

Example: replica removal

For a replica, you can remove it with add-node and del-node without moving slots because replicas do not own slots. Still, ensure you are not removing the only replica of a master if you require redundancy.

Key Takeaway

Always migrate slots from a master first; then del-node will succeed and the cluster remains consistent.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Health Checks
Definition

Verify cluster status and slots

Use CLUSTER INFO for a quick summary, CLUSTER NODES for per-node roles and slot assignment, and redis-cli --cluster check for a thorough verification.

# summary
redis-cli -p 7000 CLUSTER INFO

# detailed node list
redis-cli -p 7000 CLUSTER NODES

# guided check
redis-cli --cluster check 127.0.0.1:7000
What to watch for
  • Unreachable nodes or FAIL flags
  • Masters owning unexpected slot ranges
  • Replicas with high replication lag
Troubleshooting steps
  1. Run redis-cli --cluster check to detect configuration issues
  2. Run CLUSTER NODES to inspect node ids and slot ownership
  3. If slots are missing, inspect logs and node config files
Quick Tip

After any topology change, immediately run a cluster check to detect mismatches early.

screens.title: Common operational mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: During cluster operations several recurring mistakes appear. First, running fewer than three masters undermines quorum and prevents reliable failover. Second, forgetting cluster-enabled yes or reusing the same cluster-config-file across instances leads to node identity conflicts. Third, attempting node removal without resharding causes del-node to fail. Fourth, resharding without watching replication lag can saturate replication and lead to degraded performance. Recovery steps start with careful inspection: use CLUSTER NODES to read node ids and slot ownership, run redis-cli --cluster check for a summary of issues, and reshard or add replicas as needed. Always plan maintenance windows for resharding or node removal, and test operations in a local 6-node setup before doing them in production. A concrete recovery example: if you discover a master with unexpected slots, avoid immediate deletion — reshard slots to other masters, monitor replication, then use del-node. Key takeaway: follow the correct sequence: configure, create, monitor, then maintain with resharding and safe removal. Common operational mistakes means avoid configuration and sequence errors by following the safe steps: configure unique files, create, verify, reshard, then remove nodes.. In practical terms, what to avoid and how to recover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Operational Mistakes

Common operational mistakes and recovery

Recognize frequent errors and the safe steps to fix them without causing data loss or extended downtime.

Mistake: too few masters

Running fewer than three masters prevents quorum and reliable failover. Recovery: add masters and reshard slots to reach three or more masters.

Mistake: shared config file

Using the same cluster-config-file across instances breaks node identity. Recovery: stop misconfigured instances, correct redis.conf to unique files, restart and rejoin nodes properly.

Mistake: del-node too soon

Attempting to delete a master with slots causes failure. Recovery: reshard its slots away, confirm zero slots, then run del-node.

Mistake: reshard without monitoring

Resharding during peak load can cause lag. Recovery: perform during off-peak times and watch replication lag metrics while moving slots.

Key Takeaway

Sequence and monitoring are how you prevent and recover from cluster operational issues.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core ideas to remember. First, a functional Redis Cluster needs at least three masters for quorum, and each master should ideally have a replica for high availability. Second, every instance must use cluster-enabled yes and a unique cluster-config-file so node identities remain distinct. Third, use redis-cli --cluster create with all node addresses and --cluster-replicas to initialize a cluster and let the helper assign slots and replicas. Fourth, maintenance operations follow a clear sequence: add-node to join, reshard to move slots and balance load, and only remove a master after migrating its slots with del-node. Finally, use CLUSTER INFO, CLUSTER NODES, and redis-cli --cluster check to monitor and verify cluster health. These short reminders map directly to commands and checks you'll perform in the lab and on production systems.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a clear, practical understanding of Redis Cluster deployment and day-to-day management. You will learn the minimum topology required for a functional cluster, how to start Redis instances in cluster mode, and how to use the redis-cli cluster subcommands to create a cluster, add nodes, and rebalance data. I will show you concrete commands and configuration fragments so you can reproduce a test cluster on your machine. We will also cover common operational tasks: adding masters and replicas, resharding hash slots when capacity changes, removing nodes safely, and basic health checks. Along the way, I will highlight typical mistakes to avoid, such as insufficient master quorum, misconfigured cluster files, and attempting node removal without resharding. By the end you should be able to create a minimal 3-master, 3-replica cluster, verify its health, and perform safe maintenance operations. Think about when you might need to add capacity or replace hardware — those operations will be familiar after this chapter.

These objectives map to practical skills you will practice during the hands-on lab. First, you will identify the minimum cluster topology and explain why three masters are required for quorum. For instance, with three masters a single master failure still leaves a majority for failover decisions. Second, you will perform an initial cluster creation using the redis-cli --cluster create flow, including how to supply node addresses and set --cluster-replicas. You will learn to verify the cluster after creation using CLUSTER NODES and redis-cli --cluster check. Third, you will add new masters and replicas to a running cluster and understand the subsequent resharding step needed to move hash slots. Fourth, you will perform safe removal of nodes after migrating slots and run common health checks. Each objective includes a small milestone you can verify: create a 3-master, 3-replica test cluster; add one master and reshard; add one replica to a specific master; and run the cluster check to confirm healthy slots. Mastery comes from repeating these operations and observing cluster state.

This follow-up objectives slide outlines the practical checkpoints you'll use in the lab. For topology, confirm you can draw or list three masters and their replicas and explain how replica promotion preserves availability. For initial creation, practice starting six Redis instances with cluster-enabled yes and unique cluster-config-file entries, then run redis-cli --cluster create with --cluster-replicas 1 and accept the proposed mapping. For adding nodes, join a node using add-node and then reshard slots until the new master holds slots; verify with CLUSTER NODES. For safety and troubleshooting, practice redis-cli --cluster check and CLUSTER INFO to confirm nodes are reachable and slots are distributed. Each checkpoint prevents common mistakes: insufficient masters, missing cluster-enabled, or trying to remove a master before moving its slots. These practice objectives help you turn commands into operational habits.

A core principle of Redis Cluster is quorum-based failover. In plain terms, the cluster needs at least three masters so that a majority can be reached during failover decisions. If you run fewer than three masters, the cluster cannot reliably elect a new master when one fails. For high availability in production, each master should have at least one replica. That means a minimal robust deployment is three masters plus three replicas. The replicas follow different masters so the loss of one physical host does not remove both a master and its only replica. A common test topology uses six instances on one machine with ports 7000–7005: masters on 7000–7002 and replicas on 7003–7005. This configuration lets you observe replica promotion and slot redistribution without needing multiple hosts. A common misconception is that replicas alone provide quorum — they do not. Only masters participate in voting for failover. Key takeaway: plan for at least three masters and pair replicas across different hosts when possible. How would your promotion strategy change if two masters failed at once? Minimum Cluster Size and Topology means at least three masters are needed so a majority can be reached for failover decisions; replicas supply availability but do not form quorum.. In practical terms, why three masters and replicas matter for failover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Before you create a cluster, every Redis instance must be configured for cluster mode. The three mandatory settings you will use are cluster-enabled yes, cluster-config-file with a node-unique filename, and cluster-node-timeout set to a reasonable value. The cluster-config-file is where each node stores its local view of peers and slot assignments; Redis manages it automatically, so do not edit it while the node runs. For a test topology on one machine, create six redis. conf files that differ by port, pidfile, logfile, dbfilename, dir, and cluster-config-file. Understanding the difference between master and replica is fundamental. A master owns a subset of hash slots and accepts writes for keys mapped to those slots; replicas hold copies of a master's data and remain read-capable depending on your client setup. Masters participate in quorum voting used for failover decisions; replicas do not vote. In practice, replicas are promoted to masters when their master fails and the cluster elects a replica that can take over.
